title: As a person's faith is, so is the person

verses.sa: अर्जुन उवाचये शास्त्रविधिमुत्सृज्य यजन्ते श्रद्धयाऽन्विताः । तेषां निष्ठा तु का कृष्ण सत्त्वमाहो रजस्तमः ॥
verses.tr: Arjuna says: O Krishna, what is the standing of those who worship with faith while setting aside the rules of scripture? Is it sattvic, rajasic, or tamasic?
verses.speaker: Arjuna

intro.text: Arjuna asks Krishna what kind of faith rules those who worship with devotion while setting aside the rules of scripture.

body.text: Arjuna says: O Krishna, what is the standing of those who worship with faith while setting aside the rules of scripture? Is it sattvic, rajasic, or tamasic? Arjuna asks what quality rules people who worship with faith while setting aside scriptural rules. Krishna answers that this faith is born of a person's own nature and then describes the three kinds.

verses.sa: श्री भगवानुवाचत्रिविधा भवति श्रद्धा देहिनां सा स्वभावजा । सात्त्विकी राजसी चैव तामसी चेति तां श्रृणु ॥
verses.tr: The faith of embodied beings is born of their nature. It is of three kinds: sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic. Listen to this.
verses.angle: Shraddha is born of nature, not choice
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: In Chapter 17, Arjuna asks why people worship in such different ways. Krishna begins his answer with a single idea.

body.text: The faith of embodied beings is born of their nature. It is of three kinds: sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic. Listen to this. Krishna does not call faith a choice. He says it is born of nature, shradha, and that it is threefold, sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic. Krishna tells Arjuna that a person is made of faith, and whatever a person trusts, that is what they become.

verses.sa: सत्त्वानुरूपा सर्वस्य श्रद्धा भवति भारत । श्रद्धामयोऽयं पुरुषो यो यच्छ्रद्धः स एव सः ॥
verses.tr: O Bharata, each person's trust matches their inner nature. A person is made of trust; whatever trust he holds, that is what he becomes.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna sets aside the battlefield and speaks directly to the nature of the listener.

body.text: O Bharata, each person's trust matches their inner nature. A person is made of trust; whatever trust he holds, that is what he becomes. Listen to one word, shraddhamayah, made of trust. The verse says a person is made of trust, and whatever a person trusts in, that is what they become. Krishna now names the three kinds of people and what they worship.

verses.sa: यजन्ते सात्त्विका देवान्यक्षरक्षांसि राजसाः । प्रेतान्भूतगणांश्चान्ये यजन्ते तामसा जनाः ॥
verses.tr: The sattvic worship radiant beings; the rajasic worship yakshas and rakshasas; the tamasic worship spirits and hosts of the dead.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna is sorting human nature into three types. Listen for the single word that names the act they all share, and how the objects of their worship divide them.

body.text: The sattvic worship radiant beings; the rajasic worship yakshas and rakshasas; the tamasic worship spirits and hosts of the dead. The word yajanate, worship, binds all three types together. Yet the objects of their worship split them into three: the clear worship radiant beings, the restless seek intermediaries, and the confused turn to spirits and ghosts. Krishna then turns from worship to the harsh austerities people perform without wisdom.

verses.sa: अशास्त्रविहितं घोरं तप्यन्ते ये तपो जनाः । दम्भाहङ्कारसंयुक्ताः कामरागबलान्विताः ॥
verses.tr: People who perform harsh austerities without scriptural guidance, driven by vanity, ego, desire, attachment, and stubbornness, are not purified by them.
verses.angle: Anvitah: joined to desire and stubbornness
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: The Gita looks at the inner state behind outward practices. Listen to the hidden motives Krishna names.

body.text: People who perform harsh austerities without scriptural guidance, driven by vanity, ego, desire, attachment, and stubbornness, are not purified by them. The word anvitah means endowed with or joined to. These people are joined to desire, attachment, and stubborn force, which is why their severe austerities do not purify them. Krishna then names the ultimate consequence of such misguided self-punishment.

verses.sa: कर्षयन्तः शरीरस्थं भूतग्राममचेतसः । मां चैवान्तःशरीरस्थं तान्विद्ध्यासुरनिश्चयान् ॥
verses.tr: Those who are ignorant and perform terrible austerities without scriptural guidance, wasting away the body’s elements and Me dwelling within the body, should be known as having demonic resolve.
verses.angle: The body contains the divine within it
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Carry on from the last verse, where Krishna called out false worship; now he turns to false fasting. Listen for who suffers.

body.text: Those who are ignorant and perform terrible austerities without scriptural guidance, wasting away the body’s elements and Me dwelling within the body, should be known as having demonic resolve. Notice the word antahsharirastham, the one dwelling within the body. The text says these people waste away the very elements of the body, and they also harm Me, the one dwelling within it. Krishna now turns to the food a person eats, and how that too is divided into three kinds.

verses.sa: आहारस्त्वपि सर्वस्य त्रिविधो भवति प्रियः । यज्ञस्तपस्तथा दानं तेषां भेदमिमं श्रृणु ॥
verses.tr: Food, sacrifice, charity, and austerity are each of three kinds. Listen to these distinctions.
verses.angle: Trividhah: the word that sets up the threefold nature
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna has just condemned lawless austerity. Now he asks Arjuna to listen to something that sounds simple but is not.

body.text: Food, sacrifice, charity, and austerity are each of three kinds. Listen to these distinctions. The word trividhah, threefold, appears in this verse. It tells us that even food and sacrifice are not single things but come in three varieties, and we are about to hear what they are. Krishna now begins to describe the threefold nature of food, starting with what the sattvic person finds dear.

verses.sa: आयुःसत्त्वबलारोग्यसुखप्रीतिविवर्धनाः । रस्याः स्निग्धाः स्थिरा हृद्या आहाराः सात्त्विकप्रियाः ॥
verses.tr: Foods that increase life, purity, strength, health, happiness, and cheerfulness, and are tasty, smooth, firm, and pleasing, are dear to the sattvic person.
verses.angle: rasya and snigdha define sattvic food
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna shifts from the battlefield to the kitchen, explaining the food that steadies a clear mind. Listen for the qualities that define this sattvic diet.

body.text: Foods that increase life, purity, strength, health, happiness, and cheerfulness, and are tasty, smooth, firm, and pleasing, are dear to the sattvic person. The word rasya means tasty, pointing to food that is rich and nourishing. The word snigdha, smooth, points to food that is unctuous and easy on the body. Krishna now turns to the food that feeds a passionate nature, which is bitter, sour, and painful. Listen to how he names its effects.

verses.tr: Bitter, sour, salty, overly hot, pungent, dry, and burning foods are dear to the passionate person. They bring pain, grief, and illness.
verses.angle: Burning foods are dear to the passionate
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna contrasts the foods that build health with the foods that destroy it. Listen for the specific quality that makes the rajasic person choose these foods.

body.text: Bitter, sour, salty, overly hot, pungent, dry, and burning foods are dear to the passionate person. They bring pain, grief, and illness. Bitter, sour, salty, very hot, pungent and dry foods please the rajasic, and bring pain and illness. Krishna now turns to the tamasic pattern, describing the foods that dull the senses and cloud the mind.

verses.sa: यातयामं गतरसं पूति पर्युषितं च यत् । उच्छिष्टमपि चामेध्यं भोजनं तामसप्रियम् ॥
verses.tr: Food that is half-cooked, tasteless, foul-smelling, stale, leftover, and impure is dear to people ruled by tamas.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna has just described the restless food of passion, and now he names the diet of tamas: stale, lifeless, and foul. Listen for what this reveals about the mind.

body.text: Food that is half-cooked, tasteless, foul-smelling, stale, leftover, and impure is dear to people ruled by tamas. The word gatarasam means devoid of taste. It shows that tamas is a lifeless state, where even flavor has faded from the food and the mind. Next, Krishna describes the sacrifice of those who act without desire for reward. They offer it simply because it must be done.

verses.sa: अफलाकाङ्क्षिभिर्यज्ञो विधिदृष्टो य इज्यते । यष्टव्यमेवेति मनः समाधाय स सात्त्विकः ॥
verses.tr: A sacrifice performed according to scriptural rule by people without desire for reward, with the mind settled on “it must be done,” is sattvic.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna turns from the food people eat to the action they perform. Listen to how he defines the purest kind of offering.

body.text: A sacrifice performed according to scriptural rule by people without desire for reward, with the mind settled on “it must be done,” is sattvic. Sattvic sacrifice follows the rule, wants no reward, and rests on one thought: this ought to be done. Krishna then turns to the next kind of sacrifice, one performed for reward or show.

verses.sa: अभिसंधाय तु फलं दम्भार्थमपि चैव यत् । इज्यते भरतश्रेष्ठ तं यज्ञं विद्धि राजसम् ॥
verses.tr: But, best of the Bharatas, know that sacrifice to be rajasic when it is performed for reward or for show.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: How do you know if a good deed is really good? Krishna gives one test. Listen for the motive behind the action.

body.text: But, best of the Bharatas, know that sacrifice to be rajasic when it is performed for reward or for show. The word dambhartha, for display, is what exposes the ego. A sacrifice done to be seen is classified as rajasic, driven by restlessness and a desire for reward. Krishna then names the third kind of sacrifice, one that is performed without faith, rule, or care.

verses.sa: विधिहीनमसृष्टान्नं मन्त्रहीनमदक्षिणम् । श्रद्धाविरहितं यज्ञं तामसं परिचक्षते ॥
verses.tr: They call a sacrifice dark when it lacks scriptural rule, food offering, mantra, fee, and trust.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna is describing the lowest kind of sacrifice, one that misses every essential element. Listen to what a ritual without trust actually looks like.

body.text: They call a sacrifice dark when it lacks scriptural rule, food offering, mantra, fee, and trust. Listen to the word tamasam, dark. A sacrifice without rule, food, mantra, fee, or trust is a dark, lifeless act that leaves the worshipper unchanged. Next, Krishna moves from sacrifice to a different kind of discipline, the austerity of the body.
